clauses.heading: Compensation
clauses.text: The Company shall pay the Employee a gross annual salary of INR 8,00,000 (Rupees Eight Lakhs Only), payable in twelve equal monthly instalments, subject to applicable deductions.
risk_reasons: Standard compensation clause

clauses.heading: Probation Period
clauses.text: The Employee shall be on probation for a period of six (6) months from the date of joining. During the probation period, either party may terminate this agreement by giving fifteen (15) days written notice.
risk_reasons: Standard probation period
Notice period during probation is reasonable

clauses.heading: Notice Period
clauses.text: After confirmation, either party may terminate this agreement by giving ninety (90) days written notice or three months' salary in lieu thereof. The Employee shall not be entitled to any notice pay-out if terminated for cause.
risk_reasons: 90 days is at the higher end for mid-level roles
Asymmetric: employer can terminate for cause without notice pay

clauses.heading: Training Bond
clauses.text: The Employee agrees to serve the Company for a minimum period of two (2) years from the date of completion of any training programme. In the event the Employee resigns or is terminated for cause before the completion of the bond period, the Employee shall be liable to pay the Company an amount of INR 3,00,000 (Rupees Three Lakhs Only) as liquidated damages towards training costs incurred.
risk_reasons: Two-year lock-in period restricts mobility
INR 3,00,000 penalty may be disproportionate to actual training costs
Bond applies even if terminated for cause — unusual provision
No cap on training cost or proportional reduction over time

clauses.heading: Non-Compete
clauses.text: For a period of twelve (12) months following the termination of employment for any reason, the Employee shall not, directly or indirectly, engage in, be employed by, or provide services to any business that competes with the Company within India.
risk_reasons: 12-month post-termination non-compete
Covers all of India — extremely broad geographic scope
Applies regardless of reason for termination
Likely unenforceable under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act

clauses.heading: Confidentiality
clauses.text: The Employee shall not, during the term of employment or at any time thereafter, disclose to any third party any confidential information, trade secrets, or proprietary data of the Company without prior written consent.
risk_reasons: Standard confidentiality clause
Perpetual duration is common for trade secrets

clauses.heading: Intellectual Property Assignment
clauses.text: All intellectual property, inventions, designs, and works created by the Employee during the course of employment shall be the sole and exclusive property of the Company. The Employee hereby assigns all rights, title, and interest in such works to the Company.
risk_reasons: Broad IP assignment covering all work during employment
Does not distinguish between work-related and personal projects
No carve-out for prior inventions

clauses.heading: Dispute Resolution
clauses.text: Any dispute arising out of or in connection with this agreement shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts in Bengaluru, Karnataka.
risk_reasons: Standard jurisdiction clause
Single city jurisdiction may be inconvenient if employee is based elsewhere

enforceability_flags.explanation: Post-termination non-compete clauses are generally void under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which declares agreements in restraint of trade void to that extent. Indian courts have consistently held that post-employment non-compete restrictions are unenforceable, as distinguished from restraints during the term of employment.

findings.title: Post-Termination Non-Compete Is Likely Void
findings.body: The non-compete clause (Clause 5) restricts you from working in any competing business across India for 12 months after leaving. Under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, agreements in restraint of trade are void to that extent. Indian courts have consistently distinguished between non-compete obligations during employment (generally permissible) and those that extend beyond the employment term (generally void).

citations.quote: For a period of twelve (12) months following the termination of employment for any reason, the Employee shall not, directly or indirectly, engage in, be employed by, or provide services to any business that competes with the Company within India.
Every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void.

findings.title: Training Bond Penalty May Be Disproportionate
findings.body: The training bond (Clause 4) requires payment of INR 3,00,000 if you leave within two years of training. Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, a court may reduce this amount if it is disproportionate to the actual training costs incurred by the employer. The employer would need to demonstrate that the stipulated amount reasonably reflects actual expenses.

citations.quote: In the event the Employee resigns or is terminated for cause before the completion of the bond period, the Employee shall be liable to pay the Company an amount of INR 3,00,000 (Rupees Three Lakhs Only) as liquidated damages towards training costs incurred.

When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named.

findings.title: Notice Period Is 90 Days — Longer Than Typical
findings.body: After confirmation, resignation requires 90 days' written notice or forfeiture of three months' salary. This is significantly longer than the 30-day standard common in non-managerial roles. Additionally, if terminated for cause, you would not receive any notice pay-out — this creates an asymmetry in the notice provisions.

findings.title: Consider Negotiating These Three Points
findings.body:
Based on the analysis, three areas present the most significant exposure:

1. **Non-compete clause (Clause 5)**: One option is to request removal of the post-termination restriction entirely, or to limit it to direct competitors and a specific city. While this clause may be void under Indian law, its presence could create uncertainty.

2. **Training bond amount (Clause 4)**: One option is to request a proportional reduction mechanism — for example, if you complete 18 of 24 months, the recoverable amount reduces by 75%. Another option is to request an itemized breakdown of the training costs the bond covers.

3. **Notice period (Clause 3)**: One option is to negotiate the notice period down to 60 days, which remains reasonable while giving you more flexibility.

These are options to consider, not directives. Confirm with a lawyer before making requests.
